title: Level 1 Capstone — My English Life
overview: No new grammar. This unit asks you to use what you have, all of it, in three pieces of real work: a portfolio of your own writing, a spoken presentation about your own life, and an exit assessment that covers the whole level. It also teaches one genuinely new thing, which is how to find your own errors — because from here on there is more English than any course can cover, and the skill that matters most is being able to correct yourself.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. It maps the level rather than adding to it.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is your map. Card 2 is the only new thing in the unit.
Learn the words. Twenty, in four groups — the language of reviewing your own work.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a completed self-assessment record.
Do the Practice. Practice 1 is the diagnostic for the whole level.
Build the portfolio and record the presentation.
Take the exit assessment, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This unit teaches almost no new English, and that is deliberate. What it does is ask you to use everything at once, which is a different skill from using one pattern at a time.
Let me map the level first, so you can see the shape of what you have.
Units 0 to 9 were A1. You learned to say who you are, what you have, what you can do, how things compare, what happens generally, how to follow and give instructions, how to describe what is wrong with you, how to shop, and how to find your way. By the end of Unit 9 you could handle a day.
Units 10 to 18 were A2, and they added time depth. Unit 10 gave you the present continuous, for now and for arrangements. Unit 11 gave you obligation with have to. Unit 12 gave you the top of the comparison scale and adverbs. Unit 13 gave you will, and reasons and results. Unit 14 opened the past. Unit 15 sorted out the three futures. Unit 16 gave you the question system. Unit 17 gave you prohibition and how to read a sign. Unit 18 gave you the language of getting things fixed.
That is nineteen units, seventy-one patterns and five hundred and fifty-two words. It is more than it feels like, and most learners at this point substantially underestimate what they have.
Now, six things carry more weight than the rest, and if you are going to revise anything, revise these.
One. The present simple and the third-person -s, from Units 3 and 5. Every sentence about what generally happens uses it.
Two. The past simple, from Unit 14. The twenty irregulars and the did rule. Most of what you will say about your own life is in the past.
Three. The three futures and how to choose, from Unit 15.
Four. The question system, from Unit 16. Everything you do not know, you will have to ask for.
Five. Have to and must not, from Units 11 and 17. Opposite meanings, one word apart, and both appear where getting it wrong is expensive.
Six. The habit of confirming — repeating an arrangement, a route or an instruction back. That is not grammar and it has saved you more trouble than any single pattern.
Now the one new thing in this unit, and it matters more than any of the above.
From here, you will meet more English than any course can teach you. That is not a problem to be solved; it is simply the situation. What decides how fast you improve from now on is whether you can find your own errors.
Here is how, and it is a method rather than a rule.
Record yourself. Two minutes, on anything. Then listen back, and this is the part people skip — listen twice. Once for meaning, once for form. You cannot hear both at the same time, and trying to is why listening back feels useless when people first try it.
On the second listening, write down every place you hesitated. Hesitation is the most reliable signal you have. It marks the exact point where you were not sure, and it is far more useful than an error you did not notice, because you already know something is wrong there.
Then sort what you find into two lists. Things you know but did not do — the -s you dropped, the article you missed. Those are practice, not learning. And things you do not know — a word you needed and did not have, a structure you avoided. Those are your next lesson.
That second list is the valuable one. It is written by you, about you, and no course can produce it. The first list just needs repetition.
One more thing about avoiding. Watch for what you did not say. If you wanted to describe something that happened and found yourself using the present because the past felt risky, that is invisible in a recording unless you go looking for it. Ask yourself after every recording: what did I want to say and go round?
That question, asked honestly, is worth more than most exercises.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: To look at something again in order to judge or improve it.
words.example: Review your recording twice, not once.
practice: I reviewed the whole level in a week.
Review the units you found hardest.
It is worth reviewing before the assessment.
She reviews her notes every Friday.
words.starter: Review your recording twice, not
words.tutor: Say what you would review first from Level 1, and why that one.

words.meaning: Improvement over time.
words.example: Progress is easier to see over months than over days.
practice: I have made a lot of progress.
There has been no progress this week.
Keep a record of your progress.
Progress is not always steady.
words.starter: Progress is easier to see over months than over
words.tutor: Progress has no plural. Say a lot of progress, never many progresses.

words.meaning: To get better.
words.example: My listening improved much faster than my writing.
practice: I want to improve my pronunciation.
It has improved a lot since March.
What would you like to improve?
Nothing improves without practice.
words.starter: My listening improved much faster than my
words.tutor: Say one thing that has improved and one that has not. Both are useful to know.

words.meaning: Something you are not good at yet.
words.example: My main weakness is irregular verbs.
practice: Everybody has weaknesses.
Name your weakness before somebody else does.
It is a weakness I am working on.
The weakness is in the writing, not the speaking.
words.starter: My main weakness is
words.tutor: Say one weakness plainly. Naming it is the first step to fixing it.

words.meaning: Something you are good at.
words.example: My strength is that I ask when I do not understand.
practice: Play to your strengths.
That is a real strength.
My strengths and weaknesses are quite different.
Listening is my strongest skill.
words.starter: My strength is that I ask when I do not
words.tutor: Say a strength that is a habit rather than a skill. Those are the durable ones.

words.meaning: To study something again before an assessment.
words.example: Revise the six patterns that carry the most weight.
practice: I revised for two hours.
There is no point revising everything.
Revise what you avoid, not what you enjoy.
She revised the irregular verbs twice.
words.starter: Revise the six patterns that carry the most
words.tutor: Say what you would revise, and be honest — it should be what you avoid.

words.meaning: A short piece of writing to help you remember.
words.example: Make a note of every hesitation.
practice: I keep notes on the words I forget.
There is a note on the back of the form.
Read your notes before you record.
My notes are not organised at all.
words.starter: Make a note of every
words.tutor: Say make a note, not do a note. English uses make here.

words.meaning: To store sound, or to write something down officially.
words.example: Record two minutes, then listen twice.
practice: I record myself every week.
Record what you did, not what you meant to do.
The record is kept for three years.
Nothing was recorded.
words.starter: Record two minutes, then listen
words.tutor: Record is a verb and a noun, and they are stressed differently. Say both.

words.meaning: To learn something so you can produce it without thinking.
words.example: Memorise the twenty irregular verbs as pairs.
practice: I memorised the frame and it saved me.
There is no need to memorise everything.
She memorised it in an evening.
Memorising is not the same as understanding.
words.starter: Memorise the twenty irregular verbs as
words.tutor: Say what is worth memorising and what is not. Fixed frames are; grammar rules are not.

words.meaning: The energy you put into doing something.
words.example: It takes less effort than it did in January.
practice: Make an effort to record every week.
It is worth the effort.
The effort is the same; the result is better.
No effort is wasted here.
words.starter: It takes less effort than it did in
words.tutor: English says make an effort. Say it twice.

words.meaning: To show or explain something to other people.
words.example: Present your three minutes without reading from a page.
practice: She presented it very clearly.
I have to present on Thursday.
Present the facts first, the opinion last.
He presents once a month.
words.starter: Present your three minutes without reading from a
words.tutor: Say present as a verb and present as a noun. The stress moves.

words.meaning: The people listening to you.
words.example: Decide who your audience is before you start.
practice: The audience could not hear him.
Know your audience.
It was a small audience.
The audience asked three questions.
words.starter: Decide who your audience is before you
words.tutor: Say who your audience would be for a three-minute talk about your life.

words.meaning: To say at the start what something will be about.
words.example: Introduce the three things you are going to cover.
practice: Let me introduce myself.
She introduced the topic in one sentence.
Introduce it, then explain it.
He forgot to introduce the second part.
words.starter: Introduce the three things you are going to
words.tutor: Say let me introduce myself, then do it in two sentences.

words.meaning: To give the main points briefly.
words.example: Summarise in three sentences at the end.
practice: Can you summarise what happened?
She summarised it in one line.
Summarise before you conclude.
It is hard to summarise briefly.
words.starter: Summarise in three sentences at the
words.tutor: Summarise a whole unit of this course in one sentence. It is harder than it sounds.

words.meaning: To finish, or to decide something after thinking.
words.example: Conclude with what you will do next.
practice: I concluded that it was not worth it.
She concluded her talk with a question.
Conclude clearly — do not just stop.
What did you conclude?
words.starter: Conclude with what you will do
words.tutor: Say a closing sentence for a three-minute talk. Do not just stop talking.

words.meaning: To judge the quality or level of something.
words.example: Assess your own recording before anybody else does.
practice: It is hard to assess your own work.
The assessment is at the end of the unit.
Assess it against the descriptors.
She assessed it honestly.
words.starter: Assess your own recording before anybody else
words.tutor: Say assess and the noun assessment. Both appear in this unit.

words.meaning: Correct in every detail.
words.example: Accurate is not the same as fluent.
practice: The report was accurate.
I am more accurate in writing than in speech.
It is roughly accurate.
Accurate but slow is a normal stage.
words.starter: Accurate is not the same as
words.tutor: Say the difference between accurate and fluent. You can be either without the other.

words.meaning: Speaking smoothly, without stopping.
words.example: I am more fluent than accurate at the moment.
practice: She is fluent in three languages.
Fluent does not mean perfect.
He became more fluent after six months.
Fluent speech has errors in it.
words.starter: I am more fluent than accurate at the
words.tutor: Say whether you are more fluent or more accurate. Most people are clearly one.

words.meaning: To pause because you are not sure.
words.example: Every hesitation marks something worth looking at.
practice: I hesitated before the past tense.
Do not hesitate to ask.
She hesitated twice in three minutes.
The hesitation was in the same place both times.
words.starter: Every hesitation marks something worth looking
words.tutor: Say where you hesitate most. It is usually the same structure every time.

words.meaning: Something you are trying to achieve.
words.example: My goal for Level 2 is to stop avoiding the past tense.
practice: Set one goal, not five.
The goal is realistic.
I did not reach my goal.
What is your goal for the next three months?
words.starter: My goal for Level 2 is to stop avoiding the
words.tutor: Say one goal for Level 2. One, specific, and about something you currently avoid.

readings.title: Listen Twice, Not Once
readings.passage:
Recording yourself is advice everybody gives and almost nobody follows, and the reason is that the first attempt feels useless. You listen back, you hear yourself, you feel uncomfortable, and you learn nothing. So you stop.
The reason it fails is that you listened once.
You cannot hear meaning and form at the same time. On the first listening your attention goes to what you said and how you sounded, and the grammar passes straight through. That is not a failure of concentration; it is how listening works.
So listen twice. The first time, for meaning only — did that make sense, would somebody understand it. Then again, for form — the endings, the tenses, the small words.
On the second listening, mark every hesitation. Not every error; every hesitation. Hesitation is the most reliable signal you have, because it marks the exact moment you knew you were unsure. An error you sailed past confidently is harder to find and, in the short term, less useful. A hesitation tells you where to look.
Then sort what you find into two lists.
Things you know but did not do. The -s you dropped, the article you missed, the past form you know perfectly well. These are not learning problems. They are speed problems, and they fix themselves with use.
Things you do not know. A word you needed and did not have. A structure you wanted and went round.
The second list is the valuable one, and no course can write it for you, because it is a list of the gaps between what you wanted to say and what you could.
And one last question, asked after every recording: what did I want to say and avoid? Avoidance leaves no trace. It is the only error that is invisible in a recording, and it is the one that holds people at the same level for years.

readings.title: What You Actually Have Now
readings.passage:
Most learners at the end of a first level substantially underestimate what they can do, and it is worth being precise about it.
You have nineteen units, seventy-one patterns and about five hundred and fifty words. Those numbers are not the point. What they add up to is.
You can introduce yourself, describe your family, your home and your work. You can say what you can and cannot do. You can compare two things and name the best of several. You can say what happens generally and what is happening now. You can talk about the past — what happened, when, and what you had already tried. You can talk about the future three different ways and choose between them. You can ask for anything you do not know. You can follow directions, read a timetable, buy a ticket, describe a symptom, report a fault, fill in a form and read a safety notice.
That is not a small amount, and it is roughly the level at which a person can live in English rather than survive in it.
Here is what you cannot do yet, so the map is honest.
You cannot express a complicated opinion with reasons on both sides. You cannot follow a fast conversation between two other people. You cannot read a newspaper article without effort. You cannot write formally. You cannot use the perfect tenses, which is why you sometimes have to work around describing experience. And your vocabulary runs out in any specialised subject very quickly.
All of those are Level 2, and that is what Level 2 is for.
One more honest thing. At this point most people can produce more than they can understand, because production is under your control and listening is not. If real conversations feel much harder than the exercises, that is normal, expected, and not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

readings.title: Two Kinds of Not Knowing
readings.passage:
There is a distinction that changes how you should spend your time, and it is easy to state and hard to apply honestly.
Some things you know and do not do. You know the third-person -s. You know went is the past of go. In a careful sentence you produce both correctly every time. In fast speech you drop them.
This is not a knowledge problem. It is a speed problem, and it has a specific cure: use, repeatedly, under mild time pressure. Reading aloud, recording, speaking to somebody. Studying the rule again will not help, because you already have the rule — and this is why re-reading a grammar explanation for the fifth time feels productive and changes nothing.
Other things you genuinely do not know. A word that does not exist in your vocabulary. A structure you have never been taught. When you need one of these, you stop, or you go round.
This is a knowledge problem and it has a different cure: find it, learn it, use it three times in the next week.
Applying the distinction honestly is the difficult part, because the two feel identical in the moment. Both are experienced as I could not say that. The test is what happens afterwards. If you can produce the correct version once the pressure is off, it was speed. If you still cannot, it was knowledge.
That test takes ten seconds and it decides whether your next hour should be spent practising or learning. Most learners spend it learning when they should be practising, because learning feels more like studying — and practising, which feels like doing nothing new, is what actually moves the first list.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say the first attempt at recording yourself feels useless?
comprehension.a: Because people listen once, and you cannot hear meaning and form at the same time — the grammar passes straight through.
comprehension.why: The advice fails for a mechanical reason rather than a motivational one, which means it has a mechanical fix.

comprehension.q: Why mark hesitations rather than errors?
comprehension.a: Because a hesitation marks the exact moment you knew you were unsure, so it tells you where to look. An error you sailed past confidently is harder to find.
comprehension.why: Hesitation is self-reported uncertainty, which makes it the most reliable signal available to somebody working alone.

comprehension.q: What does the text say is the only error invisible in a recording?
comprehension.a: Avoidance — wanting to say something and going round it. It leaves no trace.
comprehension.why: This is the finding that requires a deliberate question afterwards, because nothing in the recording will prompt it. The text says it is what holds people at the same level for years.

comprehension.q: What does the text say you cannot do yet?
comprehension.a: Express a complicated opinion with reasons on both sides, follow a fast conversation between others, read an article without effort, write formally, or use the perfect tenses.
comprehension.why: An honest map needs both halves. Naming the limits precisely is what makes the list of achievements believable.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say production is easier than understanding at this level?
comprehension.a: Because production is under your control and listening is not — you choose your own words, and you cannot choose other people's.
comprehension.why: This explains a gap learners often read as failure. It is expected at this level and is not a sign anything has gone wrong.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between the two kinds of not knowing?
comprehension.a: One is a speed problem — you know it and drop it under pressure. The other is a knowledge problem — you have never had it.
comprehension.why: The two feel identical in the moment and need opposite responses, which is why the distinction is worth a whole reading.

comprehension.a: Try to produce the correct version once the pressure is off. If you can, it was speed. If you still cannot, it was knowledge.
comprehension.why: It converts an unanswerable question into an observable one, and it decides how the next hour should be spent.

comprehension.q: Two rows in the record have no evidence. What are they, and what should the learner do?
comprehension.a: Asking for anything I do not know, and choosing between will, going to and -ing. They should not be claimed until there is evidence, so both need a piece of work producing.
comprehension.why: A self-assessment with blank evidence is a list of hopes. The two blanks are the honest part of this document and they name the next two tasks.

comprehension.q: The evidence for reporting a fault says the landlord asked what exactly happened. Does that row support the claim?
comprehension.a: Not fully. It records a real attempt, but the follow-up question shows the second sentence of the fault report was missing.
comprehension.why: This is the most useful row in the document, because the evidence contradicts the claim and the learner wrote it down anyway. That is what an honest record looks like.

comprehension.q: The goal is to stop avoiding the past tense. Why is that a good goal?
comprehension.a: Because it is specific, it names something the learner currently avoids rather than something they enjoy, and it identifies the cause — using the present because it is faster.
comprehension.why: It is a speed problem correctly diagnosed. The learner already knows the past tense, so the cure is use rather than study, and the goal is written in a way that makes that clear.

grammar.title: Everything in Level 1, applied
grammar.explanation: A map of the level, not a lesson. Nothing here is new. Six things carry more weight than the rest, and if you revise anything, revise these.
grammar.rule:
THE SIX THAT CARRY THE MOST WEIGHT

  1  PRESENT SIMPLE + the -s   Units 3, 5
       what generally happens

  2  PAST SIMPLE               Unit 14
       20 irregulars + the did rule
       most of your own life is here

  3  THE THREE FUTURES         Unit 15
       arranged / intended / deciding now

  4  THE QUESTION SYSTEM       Unit 16
       everything you don't know,
       you have to ask for

  5  HAVE TO  vs  MUSTN'T      Units 11, 17
       not required / forbidden
       one word apart, opposite meanings

  6  CONFIRMING                Units 9, 10, 15
       repeating it back.
       Not grammar. Saves more trouble
       than any single pattern.

THE LEVEL: 19 units, 71 patterns, 552 words.
grammar.workedExample:
Take one ordinary situation and see how much of the level it uses.
You are reporting a leak to a landlord and arranging a visit.
1. Describe the fault — Unit 18: There's a leak under the sink and it's getting worse.
2. Say when it started — Unit 14, past simple: It started on Tuesday.
3. Say what you tried — Unit 14 again: I've turned the water off at the wall.
4. Ask a question — Unit 16: When can somebody come?
5. Give a purpose — Unit 18: Could it be a morning so that I don't miss work?
6. State an arrangement — Unit 10, present continuous: I'm working from home on Thursday.
7. Confirm — Unit 9: So, Thursday morning, between nine and one?
Seven sentences, six units, one ordinary phone call. That is what the level adds up to, and it is more than it feels like from inside.
grammar.mistake: Revising what you enjoy rather than what you avoid. Almost everybody re-reads the units they found satisfying and skips the ones they found hard, which is the exact opposite of useful. If you are choosing what to revise, choose the pattern you notice yourself going round in real speech.
grammar.tip: Revise what you avoid, not what you enjoy.
grammar.practice:
For each situation, name which units you would need. Do not write the sentences — just the units.
1. Telling somebody about your weekend.
2. Buying a ticket and asking which platform.
3. Explaining what your job involves.
4. Reporting a fault and arranging a visit.
5. Reading a safety notice and saying what you must not do.
6. Arranging to meet somebody who cannot do the day you suggested.
grammar.answers:
1. Unit 14 (past simple), Unit 12 (adverbs and describing), Unit 13 (because and so).
2. Unit 10 (would like, ticket window), Unit 16 (asking which platform), Unit 5 (times).
3. Unit 11 (have to, describing a job), Unit 5 (present simple), Unit 12 (adverbs of degree).
4. Unit 18 (fault description, so that), Unit 14 (when it started), Unit 16 (questions), Unit 10 (arranging).
5. Unit 17 (must and mustn't, reading a sign), Unit 11 (contrast with don't have to).
6. Unit 15 (shall we, how about, declining), Unit 10 or 15 (the future form you choose).
If any situation needed a unit you cannot remember, that is your revision list — and it was produced by a real situation rather than by working through the units in order.

grammar.title: Finding your own errors
grammar.explanation: The one new thing in this unit, and the most important. From here there is more English than any course can cover, so what decides your rate of progress is whether you can correct yourself.
grammar.rule:
THE METHOD

  1  RECORD  two minutes, on anything.

  2  LISTEN TWICE.
       first time  -> for MEANING
       second time -> for FORM
     You cannot hear both at once.
     Listening once is why this feels
     useless the first time you try it.

  3  MARK EVERY HESITATION.
     Not every error - every hesitation.
     It is the moment you KNEW you were
     unsure, so it tells you where to look.

  4  SORT INTO TWO LISTS:

     KNOW IT, DIDN'T DO IT
        dropped -s, missed article
        -> a SPEED problem. Cure: use.

     DON'T KNOW IT
        a word you lacked, a structure
        you went round
        -> a KNOWLEDGE problem.
           Cure: learn it, use it 3x.

  5  THEN ASK:
     "What did I want to say and avoid?"
     Avoidance leaves NO trace. It is the
     only invisible error, and the one
     that holds people still for years.
grammar.workedExample:
You record two minutes about last weekend.
1. Listen once for meaning. It made sense. Somebody would follow it.
2. Listen again for form. You hear: I go to the market on Saturday — present, and you meant the past.
3. Mark the hesitations. There were three, all just before a past-tense verb.
4. Sort them. Do you know that went is the past of go? Yes, easily, right now with no pressure. So this is the first list — a speed problem. The cure is use, not study.
5. Now the last question: what did you want to say and avoid? You wanted to say that the market had already closed by the time you arrived, and you could not, so you said the market was closed. That is the second list — a structure you do not have, and it is Level 2's past perfect.
One recording, two findings, and they need opposite responses. The first needs repetition. The second needs teaching.
The ten-second test decides which: can you produce it correctly now, with the pressure off? If yes, speed. If no, knowledge.
grammar.mistake: Listening once and concluding that recording yourself does not work. It does not work in one pass, and almost everybody stops there. The other error is treating every problem as a knowledge problem — re-reading the grammar explanation for something you already know, because studying feels more productive than practising. Re-reading a rule you already have changes nothing.
grammar.tip: Listen twice. Mark hesitations. Then ask what you went round.
grammar.practice:
Answer each one about your own English.
1. Why must you listen twice rather than once?
2. Why mark hesitations rather than errors?
3. Name one thing you know but drop under pressure.
4. Name one thing you genuinely do not have yet.
5. Which of those two needs practice, and which needs teaching?
6. What did you want to say this week and go round?
grammar.answers:
1. Because you cannot hear meaning and form at the same time. The first pass goes to meaning and the grammar passes straight through.
2. Because a hesitation marks the moment you knew you were unsure, so it points at the problem. Errors you sailed past confidently are harder to find.
3. and 4. Yours — but if you could not answer 4, record two minutes and ask again. The gaps are invisible until you try to speak at length.
5. Number 3 needs practice; number 4 needs teaching. The ten-second test separates them: if you can produce it correctly with the pressure off, it was speed.
6. This is the most valuable question in the unit and the hardest to answer honestly, because avoidance leaves no trace. If nothing comes to mind, you have not yet spoken at enough length to find out.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Two minutes, listened to twice
speaking.instructions:
Record two minutes about anything — your week, your work, your journey here.
Do not prepare it.
Listen back once, for meaning only. Ask: would somebody understand this?
Listen back again, for form only. Mark every hesitation.
Write the two lists: know it but did not do it, and do not know it.
Keep both lists. You will use them in Writing 2 and they are the honest basis for your Level 2 goal.
speaking.tutor: Speak for two minutes to the tutor and ask it to list your errors. Then compare its list with your own — the differences are interesting in both directions.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — One situation, six units
speaking.instructions:
Take the leak-and-landlord situation from the worked example on card 1.
Say all seven sentences aloud, in order, in your own words.
Then do the same for a different situation of your own — one that needs at least four different units.
Record both.
Afterwards, name the units you used. If you could not name them, that is fine — the point is that you used them, not that you can label them.
speaking.tutor: Describe a situation to the tutor and ask which parts of Level 1 you just used.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — The three-minute presentation
speaking.instructions:
Prepare and record a three-minute presentation called My English Life.
Cover three things: where you were with English a year ago, what you can do now that you could not, and what you want next.
Introduce the three at the start. Summarise at the end. Conclude with your goal.
Use at least one past tense, one future form, one comparison and one have to.
Do not read from a page. Notes of five words per section only.
Record it, listen twice, and if you hesitated more than five times, record it once more.
speaking.tutor: Give the presentation to the tutor and ask it three questions about your own life afterwards.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — The six patterns, out loud
speaking.instructions:
Say three sentences for each of the six patterns on card 1. Eighteen sentences.
All about your own life, none invented.
Record all eighteen.
Play back and mark which of the six produced the most hesitation. That one is your revision priority, and it was chosen by evidence rather than by preference.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you six prompts, one per pattern, and answer each without preparing.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — What I avoided
speaking.instructions:
Speak for two minutes about something complicated — a decision you made, a problem that took a while to solve, a disagreement.
Choose something you would find hard to explain even in your first language.
Record it.
Then listen twice and answer one question: what did you want to say and go round?
Write down every one. This is the only exercise in the course that finds avoidance, and it works because the topic is too hard to get through without going round something.
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor something complicated and ask it what you seemed to be trying to say.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the record aloud and judge it
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the whole self-assessment aloud, including the evidence column.
Then say aloud: which two rows have no evidence, and what the learner should do about them.
Then say why the fault-reporting row does not fully support its claim, even though it describes a real attempt.
Then say why the goal is a good one, and which of the two kinds of not knowing it addresses.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor the record and ask which claim it would question first.

writing.title: Writing 1 — The portfolio
writing.prompt:
Assemble five pieces of your own written work from Level 1.
They must come from at least four different units and must show at least four different kinds of writing — for example a description, a set of instructions, a form, a letter or complaint, and a recount of something past.
For each piece, write one line saying what it demonstrates.
Do not rewrite them. Use them as they were.
Then write one line for each saying what you would change now.
writing.model:
1. Unit 9, directions to where I live. Shows: movement words and the route shape, movements first and position last. Now I would name what is next to the door — on the left is not enough on a street of forty.
2. Unit 11, a job described in three parts. Shows: have to for requirements, and quite, very and really for what it is like. Now I would add an incident instead of a third adjective.
3. Unit 14, a day in the past. Shows: past simple, eight irregulars, and three story adverbs. Now I would check the four irregulars I got wrong.
4. Unit 18, the repair form. Shows: reading a form to the end, N/A rather than blanks, one box only. Now I would tick the urgency more honestly — I ticked nothing and it was getting worse.
5. Unit 18, the complaint. Shows: two so that clauses, two specific requests and a reply date. Now I would cut the third paragraph, which explains and does not help.
writing.length: Five pieces, two lines of commentary each
writing.criteria: Five pieces from at least four units; at least four different kinds of writing; one line per piece saying what it demonstrates; one line per piece saying what you would change; no piece rewritten
writing.support: Choose the pieces before you write any commentary. Lay all five out and check the kinds are genuinely different — most people's first five are three descriptions and two recounts, which shows range you do not have.
writing.extension: Find the piece where the gap between what it demonstrates and what you would change now is largest. That unit is your first revision.

writing.title: Writing 2 — The covering statement
writing.prompt:
Write a one-page statement to go at the front of your portfolio.
Include: what you could do with English a year ago; what you can do now that you could not; your main strength, which should be a habit rather than a skill; your main weakness, named plainly; the two lists from Speaking 1; and one goal for Level 2.
The goal must be specific and must name something you currently avoid.
Use at least one past tense, one comparison, one so that clause and one future form.
writing.model:
A year ago I could say my name, ask the price of something, and very little else. I understood almost nothing spoken at normal speed.
Now I can describe my work and what it requires, tell the story of a day in the past, ask for anything I do not know, fill in a form without guessing, and report a fault so that the right person comes. I can follow a conversation if it is directed at me. I still cannot follow two other people talking to each other.
My strength is a habit rather than a skill: I ask when I do not understand, and I repeat arrangements back. That has saved me more trouble than any grammar.
My weakness is irregular past forms. It is the same six every time — thought, heard, found, felt, knew, brought.
From my recording, the two lists were short. Things I know and dropped: the third-person -s, four times in two minutes; a and the, throughout. Things I do not have: a way to say something had already happened before something else, which I needed twice and went round both times.
My goal for Level 2 is to stop using the present tense when I mean the past. I know the past tense. I use the present because it is faster and nobody corrects me. I am going to record two minutes every week so that the habit has somewhere to show up.
writing.criteria: All six elements present; the strength is a habit rather than a skill; the weakness is named plainly and specifically; the two lists come from a real recording; the goal is specific and names something currently avoided; at least one past tense, one comparison, one so that clause and one future form
writing.support: Write the weakness and the goal first. They are the two that people soften, and softening them makes the whole statement vague. Name the actual six verbs, the actual dropped ending, the actual thing you go round.
writing.extension: Read your goal again and ask whether somebody could tell in three months whether you had achieved it. If not, it is not specific enough yet.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Judge the self-assessment
writing.prompt:
Use the self-assessment in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Which two rows have no evidence, and what should the learner do about them?
2. The fault-reporting row records a real attempt. Does it support the claim? Explain.
3. The past-tense row says counted 6 wrong past forms. Is that good evidence or bad evidence for the claim?
4. Why is the goal a good one, and which of the two kinds of not knowing does it address?
5. Write the two missing evidence lines as they should appear once the learner has done the work.
writing.model:
1. Asking for anything I do not know, and choosing between will, going to and -ing. Neither should be claimed until there is evidence, so the learner needs to produce one piece of work for each — a recording of real questions, and a set of future sentences with reasons.
2. Not fully. It records a real attempt and it is honest, but the landlord asking what exactly happened shows the second sentence of the fault report was missing. The claim is nearly true rather than true.
3. Good evidence. A claim with a counted error rate is much stronger than one without, because it shows the learner checked rather than assumed. Six wrong forms in one recording supports can tell the story of a day, with a named weakness attached.
4. It is specific, it names something the learner currently avoids rather than something they enjoy, and it diagnoses the cause correctly — using the present because it is faster. It addresses a speed problem, so the cure is use rather than study, and the goal is written in a way that makes that obvious.
5. Asking for anything I do not know — recorded five real questions asked this week, 6 June; three got the answer I actually wanted. Choosing between will, going to and -ing — twelve sentences with a three-word reason for each, 7 June; two reasons wrong.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 identifies that the evidence partly contradicts the claim; answer 3 explains why a counted error rate strengthens rather than weakens a claim; answer 5 supplies evidence lines with dates and specifics rather than assertions
writing.support: Go down the evidence column and mark each row: dated and specific, vague, or blank. Only one row is vague and two are blank, and that marking answers three of the five questions.
writing.extension: Now write the same self-assessment for yourself, with a blank left wherever you do not yet have evidence. The blanks are your next fortnight.

writing.title: Writing 4 — The exit assessment
writing.prompt:
This covers the whole level. Write full sentences throughout.
1. Describe your work or study in three parts — what you do, what it requires, what it is like.
2. Tell what happened on one real day, in six sentences, in the past.
3. Write three future sentences — one arranged, one intended, one decided as you write — and say which is which.
4. Write six questions you would ask about a job you had been offered.
5. Write one rule that is required, one that is forbidden, and one that is not required.
6. Report a fault in four sentences.
7. Write two sentences comparing two places you know, one with a superlative and one with not as … as.
8. Write a short complaint with one so that clause, two specific requests and a date.
writing.model:
Model answers are not given for this task, because it is the assessment.
Check your own work against these eight points instead.
1. Three parts present, part two uses have to, part three uses a degree word. (Unit 11)
2. Six past sentences, at least four irregular forms, all correct. (Unit 14)
3. Three different forms, each labelled, and no will used for something arranged. (Unit 15)
4. Six questions, correct word order, at least four with a helper, at least one subject question. (Unit 16)
5. Must, mustn't and don't have to, each doing the right job. (Units 11 and 17)
6. Which of the five descriptions, what exactly happens, when it started, what you tried. (Unit 18)
7. A superlative with the, and not as … as with a plain adjective. (Units 12 and 4)
8. One so that, two specific requests, a date. (Unit 18)
Mark each point yes or no. Anything marked no names the unit to revise, and the unit number is beside it.
writing.criteria: All eight attempted; each self-marked against the checklist; every no matched to the unit named beside it; the resulting revision list written out
writing.support: Do all eight before checking any of them. Checking as you go changes how you write the later ones and makes the assessment less useful as a diagnosis.
writing.extension: Take the three you marked no and redo them a week later, without looking at the first attempt. Compare.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which unit would you need?
activities.instructions:
For each situation, name the units you would need. Just the units, not the sentences.
1. Telling somebody about your weekend.
2. Buying a ticket and asking which platform.
3. Explaining what your job involves.
4. Reporting a fault and arranging a visit.
5. Reading a safety notice and saying what you must not do.
6. Arranging to meet somebody who cannot do the day you suggested.
7. Describing somebody so a stranger could find them.
8. Saying what you think the weather will do.
9. Asking six things about a course before you apply.
10. Filling in a form and being unsure what a box means.
activities.answers:
1. Units 14, 12, 13.
2. Units 10, 16, 5.
3. Units 11, 5, 12.
4. Units 18, 14, 16, 10.
5. Units 17, 11.
6. Units 15, 10.
7. Units 12, 8.
8. Units 13, 15.
9. Units 16, 11.
10. Units 18, 16.
Count how many different units appear across the ten situations. It should be most of the level, which is the point — ordinary situations use the whole thing, not one unit at a time.
Any unit you could not remember when it came up is your revision list, and it was chosen by a real situation rather than by working through in order.

activities.title: Practice 2 — The two lists
activities.instructions:
Use your recording from Speaking 1.
Write two lists.
List A: things you know but did not do. For each, write the correct version now, with the pressure off.
List B: things you do not have. For each, write what you wanted to say, in your own words or with a gap.
Then count both lists and answer: which is longer, and what does that tell you about how to spend the next month?
activities.answers:
No key — they are your lists. But there are two findings almost everybody has.
List A is nearly always longer, and it is nearly always the same two or three items repeating: the third-person -s, articles, and past forms. A long List A means your next month should be use rather than study — reading aloud, recording, speaking. Re-reading the rules for items on List A changes nothing, because you already have the rules.
List B is usually short and hard to write, because the things on it are by definition things you could not say. If List B is empty, that is not a good sign — it usually means the recording was on a topic easy enough to get through without stretching. Record something harder, as in Speaking 5, and try again.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Speed or knowledge?
activities.instructions:
Write SPEED or KNOWLEDGE for each. Use the ten-second test: could you produce it correctly right now, with no pressure?
1. You said she work here.
2. You wanted to say something had happened before something else and could not.
3. You said I go to the market on Saturday, meaning last Saturday.
4. You needed a word for the thing that stops water escaping and did not have one.
5. You said did you went.
6. You wanted to give a reason on both sides of an argument and could not.
7. You left out a and the in most sentences.
8. You wanted to say how long you had been doing something and went round it.
activities.answers:
SPEED: 1, 3, 5, 7.
KNOWLEDGE: 2, 4, 6, 8.
Every SPEED item is something taught in Level 1 that you can produce correctly when you slow down — the third-person -s from Unit 3, the past simple from Unit 14, the did rule from Unit 14, articles throughout.
Every KNOWLEDGE item is Level 2. Number 2 is the past perfect, 6 is arguing with concession, 8 is the present perfect continuous. Number 4 is vocabulary, which is the one kind of knowledge gap you can close immediately.
The cure differs: SPEED items need use under mild time pressure, and studying them again will not help. KNOWLEDGE items need teaching, and no amount of practice will produce a structure you have never met.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Fill the gaps in the record
activities.instructions:
Use the self-assessment in Reading 3.
1. Write the two missing evidence lines as they should appear once the work is done.
2. Rewrite the fault-reporting row so the evidence supports the claim.
3. Add two rows the record does not have, drawn from anywhere in Level 1, with evidence.
4. Rewrite the goal so it would be even easier to check in three months.
activities.answers:
Model answers — yours will differ.
1. Asking for anything I do not know — recorded five real questions asked this week, 6 June; three got the answer I actually wanted. Choosing between will, going to and -ing — twelve sentences with a three-word reason for each, 7 June; two reasons wrong.
2. Told the landlord about the leak, 22 May. Second attempt 24 May with all four sentences — he did not ask anything further and an engineer came on the 26th.
3. Two possible rows: reading a safety notice — Unit 17 task completed 3 June, found the one line I would have misread by stopping early. And arranging to meet — arranged three real meetings this month, confirmed the place every time; twice the place had not been mentioned before I asked.
4. Record two minutes every Sunday for twelve weeks, count the past-tense verbs, and count how many came out in the present. Success is that number reaching zero for three weeks running.
Number 4 is the point of this exercise. The original goal is good, and it is still a statement of intent. The rewritten one can be checked by somebody who does not know you.

activities.title: Practice 5 — The portfolio audit
activities.instructions:
Lay out your five portfolio pieces from Writing 1.
Check three things.
Range: are there at least four different kinds of writing, or are three of them the same kind?
Spread: do they come from at least four different units, or are three from the same one?
Honesty: does each what I would change now line name something real, or does it say I would check it more carefully?
Rewrite any commentary line that fails the third test.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your portfolio.
What most people find: the range is narrower than they thought. The commonest pattern is three descriptions and two recounts, because those are the two easiest kinds and they get chosen first. If that is your pattern, swap two pieces for a form, a set of instructions or a complaint.
The second finding is the third test. Vague change lines — I would check it more carefully, I would use better vocabulary — are the sign of a piece you have not actually reread. Every specific line names a sentence, a word, or a missing part, and specific lines are what make a portfolio worth keeping.

activities.title: Practice 6 — One thing, three times
activities.instructions:
Take the top item from List B in Practice 2 — something you genuinely do not have.
If it is a word, look it up. If it is a structure, note it and accept that it belongs to Level 2.
Then use it three times this week, in real situations, and write down each one.
At the end of the week, record two minutes on a related topic and see whether it comes out without effort.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: three real uses is roughly the threshold. Once is a lookup, twice is a recall, and the third time it starts to arrive on its own. That is not a rule and the number varies, but it is much smaller than people expect — the belief that a word needs twenty repetitions comes from lists, not from use.
The second finding is about structures rather than words. If your List B item was a structure belonging to Level 2, you will not be able to do this task with it, and that is the correct outcome — it tells you the item was genuinely a knowledge gap and not a speed problem. Note it, leave it, and it will be taught.

quizzes.q: Why must you listen to your own recording twice?
options: Because you cannot hear meaning and form at the same time
Because the first time is always too quiet
To count how long it is
quizzes.a: Because you cannot hear meaning and form at the same time
quizzes.why: On the first pass your attention goes to what you said, and the grammar passes straight through. Listening once is why this advice feels useless the first time people try it.

quizzes.q: Why mark hesitations rather than errors?
options: Errors do not matter at this level
A hesitation marks the moment you knew you were unsure
quizzes.a: A hesitation marks the moment you knew you were unsure
quizzes.why: It points at the problem for you. An error you sailed past confidently is harder to find, because nothing in the recording flags it.

quizzes.q: You said she work here, and you can produce she works here correctly right now. What kind of problem is it?
options: A speed problem — the cure is use
A knowledge problem — the cure is study
quizzes.a: A speed problem — the cure is use
quizzes.why: The ten-second test decides it: if you can produce the correct version with the pressure off, you have the rule and need repetition, not another explanation.

quizzes.q: You wanted to say something had happened before something else and could not. What kind of problem is it?
options: A knowledge problem — the structure belongs to Level 2
quizzes.a: A knowledge problem — the structure belongs to Level 2
quizzes.why: No amount of practice produces a structure you have never met. This one is the past perfect, and it is taught in Level 2.

quizzes.q: Which error is invisible in a recording?
options: Avoidance — what you wanted to say and went round
quizzes.a: Avoidance — what you wanted to say and went round
quizzes.why: It leaves no trace, so nothing in the recording will prompt you to look for it. That is why the method ends with a deliberate question about it.

quizzes.q: Which of these is a Level 1 pattern that carries the most weight?
options: The past simple and the did rule
quizzes.a: The past simple and the did rule
quizzes.why: Most of what you will say about your own life is in the past, and the did rule removes half the irregular-verb burden. The other three options are all Level 2.

quizzes.q: What does the text say most learners get wrong when choosing what to revise?
options: They revise what they enjoy rather than what they avoid
They revise in the wrong order
quizzes.a: They revise what they enjoy rather than what they avoid
quizzes.why: Almost everybody re-reads the units they found satisfying and skips the hard ones. The useful choice is the pattern you notice yourself going round in real speech.

quizzes.q: In the self-assessment, two rows have no evidence. What does that mean?
options: The learner has not done those tasks yet, so the claims are not yet supported
quizzes.a: The learner has not done those tasks yet, so the claims are not yet supported
quizzes.why: A self-assessment with blank evidence is a list of hopes. The blanks are the honest part of that document and they name the next two tasks.

quizzes.q: The past-tense row says counted 6 wrong past forms. Is that good or bad evidence?
options: Good — a counted error rate shows the learner checked rather than assumed
Neither — the number is too small
Bad — the claim should be removed
quizzes.a: Good — a counted error rate shows the learner checked rather than assumed
quizzes.why: A claim with a number attached is much stronger than one without, and the named weakness makes the claim more believable rather than less.

quizzes.q: Reading 2 says most people at this level can produce more than they can understand. Why?
options: Because production is under your control and listening is not
Because reading is easier than listening
quizzes.a: Because production is under your control and listening is not
quizzes.why: You choose your own words and you cannot choose other people's. If real conversations feel much harder than the exercises, that is expected and not a sign anything has gone wrong.

options: Be more fluent by the end of the year.
Record two minutes every Sunday, count the past verbs, and get the number that came out in the present to zero.
quizzes.a: Record two minutes every Sunday, count the past verbs, and get the number that came out in the present to zero.
quizzes.why: Somebody who does not know you could tell in three months whether it had been achieved. The other three cannot be checked by anybody, including the person who wrote them.

quizzes.q: Reading 2 lists what you cannot do yet. Which of these is on that list?
options: Ask for something you do not know
quizzes.why: It is why you sometimes have to work around describing experience. The other three are all Level 1 and you have them.

teacherNotes.note: Two pattern cards, both with worked examples, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Writing 4 is the exit assessment and deliberately gives a self-marking checklist instead of model answers, with the unit number printed beside each point so a failed item converts directly into a revision list.

teacherNotes.type: Card 1 teaches nothing and is still necessary
teacherNotes.note: It is a map, flagged as a contrast card so the duplication check allows and prints it. Learners at the end of a first level consistently underestimate what they have, and the worked example — seven sentences, six units, one phone call — is the fastest way to show that ordinary situations use the whole level rather than one unit at a time. Practice 1 makes the same point from the other direction.

teacherNotes.type: Card 2 is the only new content and the most important
teacherNotes.note: Self-correction is the skill that determines the rate of progress from here, because from this point there is more English than any syllabus covers. The method is deliberately mechanical — record, listen twice, mark hesitations, sort into two lists — because a learner working alone needs a procedure rather than an exhortation. The listen-twice instruction is the part that makes it work and the part everybody skips.

teacherNotes.type: Speed problems and knowledge problems need opposite responses
teacherNotes.note: Reading 4 exists because the two feel identical in the moment and learners overwhelmingly treat both as knowledge problems — re-reading an explanation for a rule they already have, because studying feels more productive than practising. Practice 3 sorts eight items and its key names the Level 2 structure behind every knowledge item, so the learner sees that those gaps are scheduled rather than personal failures.

teacherNotes.type: Avoidance is the only invisible error
teacherNotes.note: Speaking 5 is the one exercise in the course designed to surface it, and it works by choosing a topic too difficult to get through without going round something — learners are told to pick something they would find hard in their first language. A learner whose List B is empty has almost certainly chosen an easy topic, and Practice 2's key says so directly.

teacherNotes.type: Why the self-assessment has blanks and a contradiction in it
teacherNotes.note: The document in Reading 3 is deliberately imperfect: two rows have no evidence, one row's evidence partly contradicts its claim, and one row carries a counted error rate. Judging it is a harder skill than completing one, and four of the ten comprehension questions turn on the relationship between a claim and its evidence rather than on English. The fault-reporting row is the most instructive, because the learner recorded the thing that undermined their own claim.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone, including the exit assessment in Writing 4, which is self-marked against a checklist. Speaking 1, 3 and 5 ask learners to record themselves at length about their own lives, and Writing 2 asks for a personal statement: those recordings and that statement are the learner's own and must never be collected, shared or entered into the app. Speaking 5 in particular asks for something complicated and possibly personal, and the task is framed so that the learner chooses the topic and keeps the recording.

selfAssessment.statement: I can talk about my own life for three minutes without preparing every sentence.
I can listen to my own English and say what I got wrong and what I still need.
I can put together a folder of my own work and say what each piece shows.
I can look at a record of somebody's progress and see which claims are actually evidenced.

assignment.title: Level 1 exit — portfolio, presentation and assessment
assignment.instructions: Three parts, and this is the assessment for the whole level. First, assemble the five-piece portfolio from Writing 1, from at least four units and showing at least four kinds of writing, each with a line saying what it demonstrates and a line saying what you would change now; put the covering statement from Writing 2 at the front, including your two lists from a real recording and one specific goal for Level 2. Second, record the three-minute presentation from Speaking 3 without reading from a page, then listen to it twice and record one further minute naming what you would change. Third, complete the eight-task exit assessment in Writing 4, self-mark it against the checklist, and write out the revision list it produces. Keep all three together.
assignment.submissionType: A portfolio, two audio recordings and a written assessment
